why_how.text: A blowout is the sudden collapse of a tire that can throw the vehicle out of control, so hold the steering wheel tightly, steer straight ahead, ease up on the accelerator, do not brake until the vehicle is under control, and then pull all the way off the road into a safe area.
If you cannot get off the road immediately after a blowout, keep driving slowly with the emergency flashers on, and remember that under-inflated tires are one of the most common causes of blowouts.

If your brakes fail, pump the brake pedal quickly, shift to a lower gear while looking for a place to slow down and stop off the roadway, use the horn and lights to warn other drivers, and use the parking brake while holding its release so you can ease off if the rear wheels lock and skid.
If the vehicle begins to skid stay calm, do not use the brakes unless you are in danger of hitting something, and concentrate on steering out of trouble.

To steer out of a skid take your foot off the gas and turn the wheel in the direction of the skid, turning right if the rear is sliding right and left if it slides left, then if the vehicle starts to skid the other way turn again toward where you want to go and straighten the wheels to regain control.

If the gas pedal sticks, concentrate on steering with your eyes on the road, try to free the pedal with your foot, and if that fails push in the clutch or shift into neutral, use the brakes, stop at the nearest safe place and turn off the ignition.

If your wheels run off the road, grip the wheel tightly, stay on the shoulder, ease off the accelerator, brake gently and slow gradually, then after slowing check behind and ahead for traffic, turn the wheels sharply onto the pavement, and the moment the wheels hit the pavement edge turn them the other way so the vehicle does not shoot across the highway.

If you suddenly lose steering control ease up on the accelerator, and if the vehicle stays in its lane wait until it slows and then brake gently to avoid changing direction, but if it heads off the road or toward a pedestrian or another vehicle brake quickly with maximum pressure.

If your headlights fail on a lighted highway get onto the shoulder or other available space as soon as safely possible, on a dark highway try the parking lights, direction signals or emergency flashers and get off the roadway, and if all lights fail stay on the roadway and slow enough to pull off safely.

If smoke comes from under the hood get off the roadway and turn off the ignition, smother the fire with dirt or sand when no chemical extinguisher is available, never use water because burning gasoline floats on it and spreads, and if the fire gets out of control move at least one hundred feet away because the gas tank may explode.

If a vehicle comes toward you in your lane, move to the right, slow down, then sound your horn and flash your headlights, and do not turn into the lane the other vehicle left because its driver may realize the mistake and swing back.

If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks look both ways for trains, and if a train is coming get out of the vehicle and go to a safe location, while if the oil pressure light comes on get off the road, turn off the engine immediately, check the oil level and add oil if needed.

In a skid you steer in the direction the rear is sliding and stay off the brakes unless a collision looms, whereas with a stuck gas pedal you shift to neutral or push in the clutch, brake and shut off the ignition.
In a brake failure you pump the pedal quickly, drop to a lower gear and apply the parking brake while holding its release so a rear-wheel lock can be eased off.
An engine fire is smothered with dirt or sand, never water, and once it is out of control you retreat at least one hundred feet because the tank may explode.

When headlights fail you leave the road at once if it is lighted, try the parking lights, signals or flashers if it is dark, and stay on the roadway only when every light has failed, slowing enough to pull off safely.
When steering fails you ease off the gas and brake gently if the vehicle holds its lane, but brake hard if it heads off the road or toward people or another vehicle.

why_how.text: To jump start a dead battery remove the vent caps from both batteries and cover the open vent wells with a cloth, turn off the lights, heater, air conditioner and radio, connect the positive post of the dead battery to the positive post of the live battery, and connect the negative post of the live battery to the engine block or frame of the vehicle with the dead battery.

Make sure the two vehicles are not touching, start the vehicle giving the jump and let it run a few minutes before starting the other, remove the jumper cables in the opposite order and replace the vent caps, and wash any battery acid off skin, eyes or vehicles immediately with water.

A basic automobile emergency kit holds a battery-powered radio and flashlight with extra batteries, a cell phone charger, jumper cables, signal flares, blankets, critical prescription medications, a basic tool kit, a chemical fire extinguisher, a properly inflated spare tire and jack, quick energy snacks, maps of the area, a compass, a multi-tool and bottled water.

A basic first aid kit holds safety pins, triangular bandages, sterile gauze pads, self-adhesive bandages, scissors, tweezers, hand sanitizer, common pain relievers, antacids, latex gloves, sunscreen, petroleum jelly, mild soap, peroxide and moistened towelettes.

Jumper cables join positive post to positive post, but the live battery's negative goes to the dead vehicle's engine block or frame rather than to the dead battery's negative post, and the two vehicles must not touch.
